hints: Look at the functional groups: you start with an alcohol and you make only alkenes C, D and E. What small molecule must have been lost?
walkthrough:
Track what is lost when alcohol becomes alkene**
Think with me: an alcohol contains $\text{C-O-H}$, an alkene contains $\text{C=C}$ with no oxygen. Passing the vapour over hot $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ removes $\text{H}$ and $\text{OH}$ from adjacent carbons as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Loss of water to form a double bond is called dehydration, which is a type of elimination.
Final answer: dehydration (elimination of water from the alcohol)

hints: Count the carbons in the skeletal structures of C, D and E to work out the carbon chain length of the alcohol.
Ask which butanol isomer can lose water in two different positions to give both but-1-ene and but-2-ene.
walkthrough:
Count the chain**
All three products C, D and E have four carbons in a continuous chain, so they are $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ butenes. The alcohol must therefore be a $\text{C}_4$ butanol, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$.

Choose the alcohol that gives all three alkenes**
If you start with butan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, you can only easily get but-1-ene. If you start with butan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$, you can remove $\text{H}$ from C1 to give but-1-ene, or from C3 to give but-2-ene as cis and trans forms. That matches C, D and E, so the alcohol is butan-2-ol.

Draw it displayed**
In a displayed formula show every single bond: $\text{H}$ $-$ $\text{C}$ $-$ $\text{C}$ $-$ $\text{C}$ $-$ $\text{C}$ $-$ $\text{H}$ skeleton with the $\text{OH}$ group clearly attached by $\text{C-O-H}$, like $\text{CH}_3$-$\text{CH}$($\text{OH}$)-$\text{CH}_2$-$\text{CH}_3$ fully expanded.
Final answer: butan-2-ol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ shown as a displayed formula with every bond and every atom, including $\text{C-O-H}$ connectivity.

hints: Compare where the double bond sits in E versus in C and D, then compare the spatial arrangement of the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups in C versus D.
Recall that cis means the two alkyl groups are on the same side of the $\text{C=C}$ and trans means they are on opposite sides.
walkthrough:
Sort by position first**
Look at E: the double bond is at the end of the chain, between C1 and C2. That is but-1-ene. In C and D the double bond is in the middle, between C2 and C3. Those are both but-2-ene, so C and D are stereoisomers of each other and positional isomers of E.

Sort C and D by geometry**
Now picture the $\text{C=C}$. In C the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups are drawn on the same side of the double bond, that bent U shape is the cis isomer. In D they are on opposite sides, that extended shape is the trans isomer. So C is cis-but-2-ene and D is trans-but-2-ene.
Final answer: C = cis-but-2-ene; D = trans-but-2-ene; E = but-1-ene

hints: Use the $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$(aq) results to decide which of G or H is acidic enough to release $\text{CO}_2$.
Use the Na(s) results to decide which compound contains an $\text{O-H}$ group but is not acidic enough for carbonate.
Combine the hydrolysis equation $\text{F} + \text{NaOH}$ followed by acid gives $\text{G} + \text{H}$ with your answers for G and H to deduce the functional group in F.
walkthrough:
Read G from the table**
G gives colourless bubbles with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$(aq), that is $\text{CO}_2$ from: $$2\text{RCOOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{RCOONa} + \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Only carboxylic acids are strong enough acids to do this. G also gives $\text{H}_2$ with Na(s) and no reaction with alkaline iodine, consistent with $\text{RCOOH}$.

Read H from the table**
H gives no reaction with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$(aq) so it is not a carboxylic acid. It does give bubbles with Na(s), so it has an acidic hydrogen as $\text{O-H}$: $$2\text{ROH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\text{RONa} + \text{H}_2$$ It also gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine, the triiodomethane test, which is positive for $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})$- or $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$- groups. Together this points to an alcohol.

Work backwards to F**
F, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$, is heated with $\text{NaOH}$(aq) then acidified to give an acid G plus an alcohol H. That is classic acid hydrolysis of an ester: $$\text{RCOOR}' + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{RCOOH} + \text{R}'\text{OH}$$ So F must contain the ester group, $\text{RCOOR}'$.
Final answer: F = ester ($\text{RCOOR}'$); G = carboxylic acid ($\text{RCOOH}$); H = alcohol ($\text{ROH}$ / hydroxy group)

hints: Recall the name of the yellow antiseptic-smelling solid $\text{CHI}_3$ formed in a positive iodoform reaction.
walkthrough:
Name the yellow solid**
A yellow precipitate with alkaline aqueous iodine ($\text{I}_2$ in $\text{NaOH}$) is always $\text{CHI}_3$. Its systematic name is triiodomethane, also called iodoform.

hints: List what H must be: an alcohol that gives a positive iodoform test, so it must contain $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})$-. With only 3 carbons total in F, what is the only possible alcohol?
Subtract the atoms of H from F ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$) plus the water added in hydrolysis to leave the formula of the acid G.
walkthrough:
Pin down H**
H is an alcohol giving a positive triiodomethane test. At AS level that means ethanol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, which contains the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})$- unit, or methanol which is negative. Methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$, cannot give $\text{CHI}_3$. So H must be ethanol: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

Pin down G by atom balance**
F is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$. Hydrolysis is: $$\text{HCOOC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HCOOH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$$ If H uses $\text{C}_2$, G must supply the remaining $\text{C}_1$ as a carboxylic acid with no iodoform reaction. That is methanoic acid, $\text{HCOOH}$. This fits perfectly: ethyl methanoate hydrolysed to methanoic acid and ethanol.
Final answer: G = methanoic acid, $\text{HCOOH}$ ($\text{HCO}_2\text{H}$); H = ethanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$)
